opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that many of them aren't sustainable in their current form, and we should say that plainly rather than pretend otherwise.

The open web was built on an implicit bargain. A publisher puts content out for free. A search engine indexes it and sends a human back to the page. That human sees ads, maybe subscribes, maybe buys something. Everything was organized around a person's attention arriving at a page.

Agents break that loop. An agent doesn't look at a banner ad. It doesn't stay on the site. It doesn't get drawn into reading three more articles. It pulls what it needs, often from many sources at once, and synthesizes an answer. The value moves to whoever does the synthesis, and the people who created the underlying knowledge see less and less of it. If that continues, the incentive to produce high-quality original content weakens. That ends up hurting the AI systems too, because they depend on a healthy supply of fresh, trustworthy information.

So I don't think the question is how to protect the old model. It's what the new arrangement looks like. A few things seem likely to me.

First, access will become more explicit and more priced. Today it's mostly binary: you block crawlers or you don't. I expect more granular mechanisms, where content can be accessed by agents under clear terms. That could mean per-request payments, licensing, or something in between. The tooling and standards for that are still immature, but the pressure is real.

Second, the web needs to be rebuilt with agents as first-class users. Most of the web's infrastructure assumes a human with a browser. When agents become the primary consumers of information, you need ways for them to discover sources, evaluate quality, access content efficiently, and compensate creators. That's a real infrastructure problem, and it's the one I find most interesting.

Third, some content becomes more valuable, not less. Content that's genuinely original, like reporting, proprietary data, expert analysis, or real-time information, is exactly what agents can't produce themselves and need most. Commodity content that just restates what's available elsewhere is in trouble. Original sources may have more leverage than they've had in a long time, if the economic plumbing exists to let them use it.

I'm cautiously optimistic. The transition will be painful for a lot of publishers, and some business models won't survive it. But there's an opportunity to build something better than ad-supported attention arbitrage, where value flows more directly to the people creating knowledge, and agents are better because they're drawing on a healthier ecosystem. Getting there means deliberately building the infrastructure for it, not just hoping the market sorts it out.

r002.rationale: The response mentions licensing as a possible access mechanism, but does not say direct licensing deals with AI labs have mainly been available to the largest content providers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of the existing models were built for a world where a human looked at a page, and that assumption is breaking. The dominant model on the open web is advertising, and advertising works because there's a human pair of eyes on the page who might click something or at least see a brand. When an agent fetches the page, extracts what it needs, and synthesizes an answer for the user, nobody sees the ad. So the value is still being created by the publisher, but the mechanism that paid for it just doesn't fire.

And this isn't hypothetical anymore. If you talk to publishers, they're already seeing crawler traffic go up and referral traffic go down. The old bargain with search was, you let us index you, and we send you traffic. That bargain is getting much weaker because the agent is increasingly the destination, not a router.

I'd separate it into a few categories though, because they're not all equally fragile. Pure ad-supported content that's largely commoditized, like a recipe site or a how-to page, is in the toughest position, because the agent can substitute for it almost completely. Subscription models with genuine differentiation, think the Wall Street Journal or a specialized research service, are more durable, because what you're paying for is access and trust, and an agent still needs that access. And then there's content that's really a byproduct of a transaction or a community, like reviews on a marketplace or discussion on a forum, where the content is a moat for the underlying business rather than the business itself.

So what replaces it? My view is that we need machine-readable economics. Today an agent hits a page and there's a binary outcome: it's either open or it's blocked by robots.txt. That's far too coarse. What we actually need is a way for a site to say, here are the terms, here's the price, here's what you're allowed to do with this, and for the agent to accept or decline programmatically. Micropayments got laughed at for twenty years because the friction of a human deciding to pay a cent was too high. Agents don't have that friction. They can make those decisions millions of times a day. So I think this is the first time the economics of per-access pricing actually works.

The other piece is that the counterparty changes. Instead of a publisher negotiating with a billion anonymous readers, they're negotiating with a handful of agent operators and model developers. That's more like a licensing market, and we're already seeing the early versions of it with content deals. The risk there is that it consolidates power in whoever runs the agents, and the long tail of the web, which is honestly where a lot of the most interesting stuff lives, gets left out because it's not worth doing a deal with. That's the thing I'd most want the industry to get right: a protocol-level answer, not a bilateral-deals answer, so that a small site has the same ability to set terms as a large one.

The last thing I'd say is that the incentive to create content for the open web doesn't go to zero, but it changes shape. People will still publish to be found, to build reputation, to influence what the agents say. What goes away is publishing primarily to monetize attention. And if we don't build the plumbing for value to flow back, the quality of what's on the open web degrades, and then the agents get worse too, because they're trained on and retrieving from that same web. So it's not charity. The agent ecosystem has a real self-interest in keeping the supply side healthy.

r001.rationale: The response says differentiated subscription content is more durable because agents still need access, but it does not express uncertainty about whether agent access leads to paid subscriptions.

r002.rationale: It describes licensing deals with agent operators and model developers, then says the long tail is left out because it is not worth making deals with, indicating that access to those deals is concentrated among larger providers.

r003.rationale: The response discusses per-access pricing and micropayments, but does not say fixed-fee licensing revenue fails to scale with AI inference usage.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental question is how the people creating valuable content get compensated when the way we consume that content changes. A lot of the web today relies on a person visiting a page, seeing ads, or becoming a subscriber. If an agent reads that page on your behalf and gives you an answer, that chain can break.

That doesn’t mean the content becomes less valuable. The agent needs something worth reading. But we need business models that connect that value back to the creator. That could involve subscriptions, licensing, or paying for access on behalf of a user. I don’t think we know yet which approaches will work across different kinds of content.

The long-term test is whether there’s still an incentive to produce something original and useful. If we make consuming information dramatically easier but undermine the economics of creating it, that’s not a sustainable outcome.

r002.rationale: It mentions licensing generally, but does not state that direct deals with AI labs have mainly been available to the largest content providers.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss fixed-fee licensing revenue or whether it scales with AI inference usage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the underlying tension is that a lot of the web is funded by human attention. You create content, people visit your site, and you monetize those visits through advertising or subscriptions. An agent can consume that content and deliver value to a user without that user ever visiting the source. So the value is still being created, but the mechanism that pays for its creation can break.

That doesn’t mean the existing models disappear overnight. But I don’t think we should assume they remain sustainable simply because agents need the content. Needing something and paying for it are different things.

The opportunity is to build mechanisms through which content creators get compensated when agents use their work. That could involve licensing, subscriptions, or payments tied to access. There’s probably no single model that works for every kind of content. The important question is whether enough of the value flows back to support creating the next piece of useful information. Otherwise, we risk making access to knowledge more efficient while weakening the incentives to produce it.
